| D-2 | major | conventions.md names both [[ ]] and (( )) and states the mechanism: failure discarded unless the construct is the enclosing function's literal last statement, a semicolon is no escape, and a loop keeps only the last iteration's result. | _working-memory/conventions.md:24 — "Under `set -e`, a failing `[[ ]]` or `(( ))` doesn't abort. The failure is discarded unless the construct is the enclosing function's literal last statement, so `f() { [[ 1 -eq 2 ]]; echo reached; }` prints `reached` and exits 0. A semicolon is no escape either (`true; [[ 1 -eq 2 ]]; echo reached` prints it too), which is why the rule is \\"never use either as a statement\\" rather than \\"never start a line with one\\". Loops are where it hides longest: `for i in 1 2 3; do [[ $i -ge 3 ]]; done` exits 0, so only the last iteration's result survives. `[ ]`, `grep`, and a function returning non-zero all propagate from every one of those positions." |
